changelog.change: Initial entry — converted from CV Intoxicating Substances Reference: the shared mu-opioid toxidrome, naloxone principles, and per-agent features for heroin, fentanyl and analogs, methadone and buprenorphine, and tramadol and loperamide.

summary: The mu-opioid toxidrome — miosis, respiratory depression, CNS depression — is remarkably consistent across the class; what differs is potency, receptor kinetics, half-life, and the non-opioid mechanisms layered on top (serotonergic for tramadol, hERG/sodium-channel for methadone and loperamide). Support ventilation first, titrate naloxone to breathing not arousal, and plan for re-sedation.
whyThisMatters: Opioid overdose is the archetypal reversible prehospital and ED death, but the reversal has traps: over-reversal buys vomiting, aspiration, and a combative dependent patient; under-observation misses re-sedation when naloxone's 30-80 minute half-life is outlasted by the opioid; and the atypical agents (methadone QT, loperamide cardiotoxicity, tramadol seizures, fentanyl wooden chest) each need a step naloxone alone does not provide.
clinicalTakeaway: Bag-valve-mask ventilate first — do not wait on the antidote. Give naloxone 0.04-0.4 mg IV/IM/IN titrated to adequate respiration, not full arousal, and observe 6-12 hours after reversal. Recurrent re-sedation → naloxone infusion (~two-thirds of the effective bolus per hour). Standard naloxone doses work for fentanyl analogs in the overwhelming majority — plan for repeat dosing and infusions, not bigger single boluses. Get an ECG in any opioid-toxic patient with a plausible methadone or loperamide history (QT/QRS), treat tramadol seizures with benzodiazepines, manage fentanyl wooden-chest with paralysis and intubation, and offer take-home naloxone plus a buprenorphine/OUD pathway to every patient before discharge.

body.text: The shared toxidrome and naloxone principles

items: Toxidrome: miosis, reduced respiratory rate and depth, CNS depression, hyporeflexia. Pinpoint pupils + depressed respiration + depressed consciousness that reverse promptly with naloxone is as close to bedside-diagnostic as toxicology offers.

Ventilate first (BVM) while preparing naloxone. Naloxone 0.04-0.4 mg IV/IM/IN, titrate to respiration (goal: breathing, not arousal — over-reversal in a dependent patient causes vomiting, aspiration, agitation).
Observe 6-12 h post-reversal (naloxone t½ 30-80 min vs longer opioid duration). Recurrent re-sedation despite boluses → naloxone infusion, typically ~2/3 of the effective bolus dose per hour.
Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema ("heroin lung") shortly after use: supportive oxygenation/ventilation, not diuretics.
Before discharge: offer take-home naloxone and a buprenorphine / OUD-treatment pathway to every patient with OUD regardless of stated interest.

rows: Prodrug → 6-MAM (heroin-specific urine marker, detectable only hours) → morphine. Track marks, skin-popping scars; noncardiogenic pulmonary edema is a recognized complication
Standard naloxone titration; observe 6-12 h. NCPE → oxygen/ventilation support, not diuretics

50-100× morphine (carfentanil ~10,000×). Rapid-onset apnea WITHOUT the gradual sedation curve, often in supply-linked clusters. Chest-wall rigidity ("wooden chest") after rapid high-dose exposure can prevent BVM ventilation

Standard naloxone doses ARE effective — but more patients need an infusion than a single bolus. Wooden chest unresponsive to naloxone → neuromuscular blockade + intubation (reversal is too slow for an obstructed airway). Fentanyl test strips as discharge counseling

Full mu agonist + NMDA antagonism + hERG K-channel blockade → QT prolongation and torsades disproportionate to opioid effect. Half-life 8-59 h, accumulates — overdose more dangerous and prolonged than single-dose potency suggests

Naloxone titrated to respiration, usually much higher cumulative doses + an infusion. Get an ECG for QTc. Torsades → magnesium, overdrive pacing / isoproterenol, correct electrolytes, avoid other QT-prolonging agents. IV buprenorphine is an emerging alternative for methadone-induced respiratory depression

High-affinity partial mu agonist with a respiratory-depression ceiling — safer as monotherapy, but precipitates withdrawal by displacing full agonists (heroin, fentanyl, methadone). Long duration (24+ h). Ceiling is lost when combined with other CNS depressants

Precipitated withdrawal in a patient on full agonists: supportive care, and — counterintuitively — continued or escalated buprenorphine dosing resolves it faster than stopping. The instinct to stop the causative drug is backwards

Weak mu agonist whose analgesia depends on SNRI activity — causes seizures and serotonin syndrome independent of any co-ingestant. Seizures in an otherwise mild opioid toxidrome point directly at tramadol

Benzodiazepines for seizures; naloxone helps the opioid component but NOT the SNRI-mediated seizure/serotonin risk. Serotonin syndrome → benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine if refractory, stop all serotonergic co-meds

Peripherally restricted at therapeutic dose; grossly supratherapeutic misuse (>100 mg/day, hundreds of tablets) saturates P-glycoprotein → CNS entry + hERG K-channel and sodium-channel blockade — a dual-channel cardiotoxicity unique among opioids here. QRS widening + QT prolongation + torsades/VT in someone using an antidiarrheal at absurd doses is the signature

Continuous cardiac monitoring, correct K/Mg. Sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening; magnesium and overdrive pacing for torsades. Treat as a sodium-channel-blocker / QT-prolonging overdose. Ask about dose, not just drug name

body.text: Do not over-anchor on "naloxone won't work on fentanyl" — it does, at standard doses, in the overwhelming majority of cases. The real practice shift is infrastructure: plan for repeat dosing and infusions. And titrate to respiration, not wakefulness.
